Framework Objects

SIMBA Objects Module

Various objects and functions to handle simulation lattices, commands, and elements.

Classes:

  • runSetup: Defines simulation run settings, allowing for single runs, element scans or jitter/error studies.

  • frameworkObject: Base class for generic objects in SIMBA, including lattice elements and simulation code commands.

  • frameworkLattice: Base class for simulation lattices, consisting of a line of LAURA elements.

  • frameworkCounter: Used for counting elements of the same type in ASTRA and CSRTrack

  • frameworkGroup: Used for grouping elements together and controlling them all simultaneously.

  • element_group: Subclass of frameworkGroup for grouping elements. # TODO is this ever used?

  • r56_group: Subclass of frameworkGroup for grouping elements with an R56. # TODO is this ever used?

  • chicane: Subclass of frameworkGroup for a 4-dipole bunch compressor chicane.

  • getGrids: Used for determining the appropriate number of space charge grids given a number of particles.

OUTPUT_LINE_SEPARATOR = '-'

Separates a line name from an element name in an output beam filename.

OUTPUT_TURN_SEPARATOR = '-t'

Separates an element name from a turn index in an output beam filename, multi-turn only.

apply_programs(turn)[source]

Set each programmed element to its value for turn.

Called at the top of every turn by the codes simba loops in Python – Ocelot, MAD-X and Bmad. Codes handing the whole program to the tracker in one go (Xsuite, elegant) set it up once instead and do not call this.

Parameters:

turn (int) – Turn number, 1-based

Return type:

None

beam_turn(turn)[source]

Which turn a beam from an output_turns() entry actually is.

None there means “the only one there is”, which covers both a single-pass line and the default multi-turn run that keeps only the last turn. Those are different turns, and this is what resolves them – it is what goes in turn, so that a beam says which turn it is even when its filename does not.

Either half of the pair can be handed in. They differ only where the name is unsuffixed, and there the answer is the same either way, so a backend that has kept only name_turn does not have to thread data_turn down beside it.

Parameters:

turn (int | None) – Either half of an output_turns() pair

Returns:

A 1-based turn number, never None

Return type:

int

check_nsuperperiods_supported()[source]

Warn when superperiods were asked for and cannot be given.

Deliberately loud: unlike most unsupported settings, ignoring this one does not make the run slower or coarser, it tracks a different machine – one Nth of the intended ring.

None

Warn when the map that came back cannot be a one-turn map.

Return type:

None

check_pass_rigidity(brho, tolerance=0.01)[source]

Warn if the tracked beam disagrees with this pass’s stated momentum.

Codes that take a field rather than a normalised strength get Brho from the beam actually loaded. The k came from the layout, resolved at the momentum that pass states.

A warning rather than a refusal.

Parameters:

  • brho (float)

  • tolerance (float)

Return type:

None

check_periodic_supported()[source]

Warn when the periodic solution was asked for and this code cannot.

Return type:

None

check_programs_fit()[source]

Warn when a program and the run do not cover the same turns.

Two ways to author a pulse that is not the one intended, both of which track perfectly: knots past the last turn, so part of the programme – usually the kick – never happens, and a last knot the run then sits on for thousands of turns, which is elegant’s ramp_elements trap written by hand.

Return type:

None

check_programs_supported()[source]

Warn when a device program was asked for and this code cannot run one.

Return type:

None

Warn when a long lepton ring is tracked with radiation switched off.

Parameters:

turns_that_matter (int) – How many turns are enough for the beam to reach equilibrium if radiation is on

Return type:

None

check_single_particle_supported()[source]

Return type:

check_superperiods_close()[source]

Warn when the declared superperiod count and the geometry disagree.

A sector is meant to be open, so the closure test in check_turns_closed() would only ever fire spuriously here. The meaningful question is whether N of them make a ring, and the net bend answers it: N * angle should be a whole number of turns.

Catches the count being wrong, which is otherwise invisible – tracking 6 sectors of a 4-fold ring runs and converges and describes a machine that does not exist.

Return type:

None

check_turns_closed(tolerance=0.0001)[source]

Warn when a line that does not close is treated as though it did.

Closure is tested on LAURA’s geometry: the first element’s entrance against the last element’s exit, to tolerance relative to the path length.

A superperiod is the legitimate exception – one sector of an N-fold-symmetric ring is open on its own and closes after N of them. Declaring nsuperperiods() says so, and the check then asks the question that is actually meaningful: whether N of these close.

Parameters:

tolerance (float)

Return type:

None

property closed_geometry: bool

Whether LAURA records this line’s reference orbit as closing.

periodic() is this plus an override, because asking for the closed optics solution is a choice; whether the machine is a ring is not. Code that needs the fact rather than the choice wants this one – MAD-X decides whether to segment at RF cavities on it (see segmentElements()), and an injection-mismatch study setting tracking: {periodic: false} on a real ring must not thereby turn its cavities into accelerating ones.

Returns:

True if LAURA’s section geometry is closed

Return type:

bool

closed_orbit: Any

The periodic orbit at the start of the line, as a 6-vector in this code’s otm_convention; see read_closed_orbit().

Element names another line in this run also writes an output file for.

paramiko.SSHClient

property end: str

Property to get the name of the ending element of the lattice. This method checks if the file block contains an “end_element” key or a “zstop” key. If “end_element” is present, it returns the corresponding element. If “zstop” is present, it iterates through the elementObjects to find the element with the matching end position. If no match is found, it returns the last element in the elementObjects.

Returns:

The name of final element of the lattice.

Return type:

str

property endObject: PhysicalBaseElement

Property to get the final element of the lattice. See end() for more details.

Returns:

The final element of the lattice.

Return type:

Element

property entrance_s: float

Property to get the s position of the lattice entrance.

start_s is the s at the exit of the first element, so its length has to come back off. The two are equal for the usual case of a lattice starting on a zero-length marker, and differ for one starting on a real element.

This is the anchor for per-element s positions, which are measured from the lattice entrance.

Returns:

S position of the entrance of the lattice.

Return type:

float

getSValues(as_dict=False, at_entrance=False, drifts=True)[source]

Get the S values for the elements in the lattice. This method calculates the cumulative length of the elements in the lattice, starting from the entrance or the first element, depending on the at_entrance parameter. It returns a list or dict of S values, which represent the positions of the elements along the lattice.

Parameters:

  • as_dict (bool, optional) – If True, returns a dictionary with element names as keys and their S values as values.

  • at_entrance (bool, optional) – If True, calculates S values starting from the entrance of the lattice. If False, calculates S values starting from the first element.

  • drifts (bool, optional) – If True, include s-values for drift elements

Returns:

A list or dictionary of S values for the elements in the lattice. If as_dict is True, returns a dictionary with element names as keys and their S values as values. If as_dict is False, returns a list of S values.

Return type:

list | dict

link_handoff_beam()[source]

Make sure the end of the line has an unsuffixed beam file.

The next section reads <end>.openpmd.hdf5 by name, and with write_turns: true a code that routes its end element through output_turns() writes only <end>-t1 … <end>-tN – so asking for per-turn output silently broke the chain to whatever line came next. Measured in Ocelot, which does route it that way.

The handoff beam is the last turn’s, which is what the default run writes under that name anyway, so this restores the invariant rather than inventing one: the unsuffixed name is always the beam leaving the line. Copied rather than linked, because the summary files use HDF5 external links and a link to a link is one more thing to go wrong.

Return type:

None

match(params)[source]

Perform transverse matching of the lattice using Ocelot’s built-in matching algorithm.

The params dictionary should contain the following keys:

  • “variables”: A list of element names (magnets only).

  • “targets”: A dictionary where keys are element names and values are dictionaries with keys corresponding to Twiss parameters (“beta_x”, “beta_y”, “alpha_x”, “alpha_y”, “eta_x”, “eta_y”, “eta_xp”, “eta_yp”, “mux”, “muy”) and their target values.

  • “start”: (optional) The name of the starting element for matching. Defaults to the first element.

  • “end”: (optional) The name of the ending element for matching. Defaults to the last element.

The matching dictionary should have this structure within the lattice file block:

files:
  line:
    <.....>
    match:
      variables:
        Q1
        Q2
        S1
      targets:
        SCR1: {beta_x: 10.0, alpha_x: 0.0}
        SCR2: {beta_y: 12.0, alpha_y: 0.0}
        SCR3: {beta_x: {mode: greaterthan, value: 8.0}}
      start: Q1
      end: SCR3
Parameters:

params (Dict) – Dictionary containing matching variables, targets, and optional start and end elements.

Returns:

Updated elementObjects if matching is successful, None otherwise.

Return type:

Dict | None

Raises:

  • ValueError – If required keys are missing in the params dictionary or if specified elements are not found in the lattice.

  • RuntimeError – If the matching process fails.

normalisation_twiss()[source]

Periodic Twiss and closed orbit for Courant-Snyder normalisation.

Handed to tune_diffusion() so a frequency map works in normalised coordinates.

property nsuperperiods: int

How many times the line is traversed per turn.

One sector of an N-fold-symmetric ring is a superperiod: it is open on its own and closes after N of them. Rather than making the user write the whole ring out N times, the sector is written once and tracked N times per turn:

files:
  RING:
    code: ocelot
    tracking: {turns: 1000, nsuperperiods: 4}

A turn stays a turn. Those settings track 4000 passes through the sector, and the beam files, the turn suffixes and anything else counted per turn still count 1000 of them. Measured against Ocelot: a sector with nsuperperiods=N is bit-identical to N copies of it with nsuperperiods=1, and both record one point per turn.

Returns:

The declared count, or 1 – which is the same as not asking.

Return type:

int

None unless the line is periodic() and the code can produce one. Read after the run by read_one_turn_map().

one_turn_map_canonical(beta0=None, magnitude=True)[source]

one_turn_map in one common convention, so codes compare.

Canonical here is Xsuite’s (x, px, y, py, zeta, delta). The conversion is a diagonal similarity D R D^-1 with D = diag(1, 1, 1, 1, d5, d6). Normalising cannot invent or destroy a tune; it can only fix the longitudinal block.

With magnitude=True (the default) it returns None where the conversion is not a rescale. Elegant’s fifth coordinate is geometric path length, not time of flight, so a drift has R56 = 0 where the other codes have L / (beta0 * gamma0)**2.

magnitude=False applies otm_longitudinal_sign alone.

Parameters:

  • beta0 (float | None) – Reference v/c. Read from the tracked beam when not given, and not needed at all when magnitude is False.

  • magnitude (bool) – Convert sizes as well as signs.

Returns:

The 6x6 map in canonical coordinates, or None when magnitude was asked for and this code’s conversion is not a rescale.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray | None

optics_summary: Any

The code’s own tune and chromaticity; see read_optics_summary().

otm_convention: ClassVar[str] = ''

The coordinate order one_turn_map is written in, as this code writes it. one_turn_map_canonical() converts it.

  • The transverse blocks need no conversion at all.

  • The longitudinal block is three different problems. Ocelot differs from MAD-X by a sign, Xsuite by a factor beta0**2, and elegant by an additive term – its fifth coordinate is geometric path length, so a drift has R56 = 0.

otm_longitudinal_scale: ClassVar[int | None] = None

Power of beta0 in the magnitude of the longitudinal conversion; see one_turn_map_canonical(). None means the conversion is not a rescale (elegant).

otm_longitudinal_sign: ClassVar[int] = 1

Sign of this code’s fifth coordinate against the canonical one (Xsuite, Bmad).

output_basename(name, turn=None)[source]

Filename stem for name’s output beam file, qualified if needed.

Output beam files are named by element alone, so they must not clash for multi-turn tracking. Qualifies only what actually collides: colliding_outputs is empty unless Framework.track found the same name written by more than one line. All colliding occurrences are qualified, including the first, so the name follows from the settings file.

turn qualifies the other axis. It is ignored on a single-turn run, so nothing changes for a lattice that does not ask for turns.

Parameters:

  • name (str)

  • turn (int | None)

Return type:

str

output_turns()[source]

(data_turn, name_turn) for each beam file a run should write.

data_turn selects which turn’s particles to write and name_turn is handed to output_basename(), so the unsuffixed single-turn name survives when only the last turn is being kept.

Return type:

list

property passes_per_turn: int

How many times this code will actually traverse the line per turn.

nsuperperiods() is what was asked for; this is what will happen, so it is 1 on a code that cannot repeat the line. Backends loop over this, and revolution_period() multiplies by it, which keeps a device program’s turn axis honest either way: on a code that ignores superperiods a turn really is one pass, and the warning from check_nsuperperiods_supported() is the thing to act on.

property periodic: bool

Whether to ask the code for the closed (periodic) optics solution.

Unlike turns(), this is not primarily a tracking setting: whether the reference orbit closes is a fact about the lattice, and LAURA already records it as section geometry (_machine_geometry()).

The tracking block overrides that either way, which is what an injection-mismatch study on a real ring needs:

files:
  RING:
    code: elegant
    tracking: {turns: 1000, periodic: false}
Returns:

True if section geometry is closed

Return type:

bool

Elements whose strength is a program over turn number.

A tracking setting, like turns(), and the half of R19 that is the study rather than the hardware – when a kicker fires and at what amplitude:

files:
  RING:
    code: elegant
    tracking:
      turns: 10
      programs:
        - element: KICK1
          turns:  [1, 4, 5]
          values: [0.0, 1.0e-3, 0.0]
          interpolation: hold

Turns are 1-based, values are in the element attribute’s own units, and the default rule is hold and is no code’s default: see simba.Modules.DeviceProgram, which is where all three of those are argued.

Synchrotron-radiation model for this line, or None for none.

mean gives damping and the energy loss; quantum adds the excitation, and only with both does an equilibrium emittance exist; None means not stated, and leaves every code on its own default – which is not the same default everywhere.

property revolution_period: float

passes * C / (beta0 * c).

C is this line’s length, and passes_per_turn() is how many times a turn crosses it – so for one superperiod of an N-fold ring this is the ring’s revolution period, which is what a program stated in turns has to be converted against.

The conversion between the two axes a device program can be stated on. simba states one in turns; elegant’s WAVEFORM and Xsuite’s t_turn_s are both in seconds, so both have to come through here.

beta0 and not c. The difference is one part in 2*gamma**2 per turn, which is nothing on turn one and a whole turn out by the time a ring study has run long enough to matter – and a kicker a turn out fires into the wrong bucket.

Returns:

Seconds per turn, or 0.0 if there is no beam to ask

Return type:

float

Type:

Seconds for one turn

ring_parameters()[source]

Tune, periodic Twiss and momentum compaction, from the one-turn map. The first two come from the raw map, and the latter comes from the canonical map.

Chromaticity is deliberately absent: it is not in a single one-turn map. It needs maps at two momenta, or the code’s own periodic Twiss.

Returns:

{} if there is no map. Otherwise tune_x/tune_y (fractional), beta_x/alpha_x/gamma_x and the y equivalents, stable_x/stable_y, and slip_factor / momentum_compaction where the convention allows.

Return type:

dict

run_command(command, logfile, **kwargs)[source]

Run a simulation code, logging to logfile, and raise if the code says it failed.

A code that gives up part-way still looks like a successful run to everything downstream, which then dies reading output that was never written – so the exit status is read here, once, for every code that runs a subprocess.

None

run_remote()[source]

Run the simulation on a remote server using SSH and SFTP, following these steps:

  1. Connect to the remote server using connect_remote().

  2. Create a subdirectory on the remote server with the same name as master_subdir.

3. Send the required files (simulation input file(s), initial beam distribution file, field/wakefield files).

  1. Execute the simulation and wait for completion.

  2. Retrieve all output files created since the start of the simulation back into master_subdir
